What Is UGC, and Why Brands Now Pay for It

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 3 August 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

UGC now means two things: genuine customer content, credible because it was not commissioned, and paid creator content styled to look organic, which performs in paid social. Use both, keep them distinct, and disclose and review the paid kind as the advertising it is. The rules are specific. The FTC's Endorsement Guides say ads that present people as actual consumers should use actual consumers or say otherwise, and its 2024 rule bans testimonials from people who never used the product.

User-generated content, UGC, originally meant exactly what it says: content made by users, customers posting photos, reviews, and videos about products on their own initiative. Brands loved it because it was credible and free. Nielsen's 2021 Trust in Advertising study found recommendations from people consumers know were the most trusted channel, at 89% of respondents.

The term has since been adopted by the advertising industry to describe something different: content produced by paid creators, deliberately styled to look like an ordinary person's post, for use in the brand's own advertising. The two meanings now coexist, and the distinction matters for both effectiveness and law.

The two kinds

Organic UGC is made by real customers, unpaid, on their own accounts. Brands can request permission to reuse it, feature it, and reward it, and it remains the most credible form of social proof available because it was not commissioned.

Commissioned UGC-style content is made by creators paid to produce it, usually not posted on the creator's own account at all but delivered to the brand for use in paid ads. The creator's following is irrelevant; what the brand is buying is the format, a person on a phone talking about the product the way a friend would, because that format performs in paid social far better than polished production does.

Organic UGCCommissioned UGC-style contentCreator post on own account
Who makes itA real customer, unpaidA paid creator, often actingA paid creator, as themselves

Why brands pay for it

Paid social platforms reward content that looks native to the feed. Studio-produced ads are identified and skipped; a person holding a phone is watched. Commissioned UGC-style content is cheap to produce in volume, fast to iterate, and allows dozens of variations to be tested against one another. For a performance programme that needs new creative every few weeks, it has become the default.

The platforms have built products around it. TikTok's Spark Ads let an advertiser promote an organic post from its own account or from a creator's account that has authorised it, with the creator choosing an authorisation period of 7, 30, 60 or 365 days when generating the code. That choice is a usage-rights decision made in an app, and it should match the contract.

The spend behind creator content is growing. The IAB put US creator ad spend at $37 billion in 2025 and projected $44 billion in 2026.

What it costs

Commissioned content is priced per piece, from a modest fee for a short video from a newer creator to considerably more from experienced UGC creators with a track record of producing ads that convert. Platforms and marketplaces exist to source and manage creators at scale. Usage rights, how long and where the brand may run the content, are priced separately and are often the larger cost.

A usage-rights clause should name four things: the channels (organic, paid social, website, connected TV), the territories, the term, and whether the brand may edit or cut the footage. A thirty-day paid social licence and a perpetual all-media licence for the same video are different purchases.

The "it looks organic" quality that makes the format effective is precisely what the disclosure rules exist to address.

The disclosure question

When commissioned content runs as the brand's own ad, in the brand's ad account, it is an advertisement and is treated as one; the person in it is effectively an actor, and the platform labels it as sponsored. Claims made in it are the brand's claims and must meet the same standards as any ad, including, in reviewed categories, the same compliance review.

The actor point has a specific rule. The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, say advertisements presenting endorsements by people represented as "actual consumers" should use actual consumers "in both the audio and video," or clearly and conspicuously disclose that they are not. A UGC-style ad scripted for a paid performer and framed as a customer's story needs that disclosure.

When a paid creator posts UGC-style content on their own account presenting it as their own opinion, it is an endorsement, and the material connection must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously under the endorsement rules that apply in most jurisdictions. The "it looks organic" quality that makes the format effective is precisely what the disclosure rules exist to address. In the UK the ASA, CAP and CMA's October 2026 guide asks for "#Ad" at the very beginning of the content and notes that AI-generated content must comply too.

Testimonial content also carries its own rules: claims about results must reflect what a typical customer can expect, or say otherwise, and fabricated or scripted testimonials presented as genuine are prohibited. The Endorsement Guides treat a result as implying typicality unless the advertiser discloses what people generally achieve, and found generic disclaimers such as "results not typical" insufficient in the Commission's testing. The FTC's 2024 rule on reviews and testimonials goes further: it bans testimonials attributed to people who do not exist, including AI-generated ones, or who had no real experience with the product, and lets the FTC seek civil penalties from knowing violators. The brand can be liable even when the creator is not.

Using it well

Brief creators on the product truth and the audience's actual doubts, and let them speak naturally; scripted UGC reads as scripted. Produce in volume and test; the format's advantage is iteration. Our playbook on campaign testing that reaches a decision covers how to set up variant tests that end in a choice.

Keep organic UGC separate and honest: feature real customers, with permission, and never edit their words into claims they did not make. The same standard runs through what makes a case study believable. Give each piece a job as well: our piece on content with a job covers naming the reader, decision and next action before commissioning.

Apply the compliance library to every piece, because a creator saying "I earned twelve percent" is a yield claim whoever says it. In UK financial services, the FCA's guidance on social media promotions expects promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading and to give a balanced view of benefits and risks, in any format. And in restricted categories, remember that the content still has to run somewhere; UGC-style creative does not open a platform that has closed the category. Our explainer on landing pages and ad review covers what happens at the review stage.

lowob takeaways

  • Keep the two kinds apart. Organic UGC is earned proof; commissioned UGC-style content is advertising.
  • Buy the rights explicitly. Channels, territories, term and edit rights, matched to any platform authorisation.
  • Do not present actors as customers. Use real customers or disclose that they are not.
  • Review every claim. Results must be typical or qualified, and yield claims are yield claims whoever says them.

Common questions

What does UGC mean in advertising?

Originally content made by customers on their own initiative. It now also means content produced by paid creators, styled to look like an ordinary person's post, for use in the brand's own advertising.

Why do brands pay for UGC-style content?

Paid social platforms reward content that looks native to the feed. UGC-style content is cheap to produce in volume, fast to iterate, and lets dozens of variations be tested against one another.

Do paid UGC creators have to disclose that they were paid?

When a paid creator posts on their own account as their own opinion, it is an endorsement and the connection must be disclosed clearly. When it runs as the brand's ad and presents the person as a customer, the FTC expects real customers or a disclosure that they are not.

Are fake or AI-generated testimonials illegal?

In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule bans testimonials attributed to people who do not exist, including AI-generated ones, or who never used the product, with civil penalties for knowing violations. UK rules also prohibit fake reviews.
